The Corsula (Rhinomugil corsula) is a mugilid fish endemic to fresh and brackish waters of the Indian subcontinent, where it supports small-scale fisheries across much of its range. Females of this species attain a maximum total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], a size that distinguishes them from several smaller-bodied congeners that rarely exceed 30 centimeters. This ultimate length is achieved through a sustained period of somatic growth that continues well beyond the onset of reproductive maturity. Field studies conducted across multiple river systems have documented gravid females approaching this asymptotic size, although most captured individuals fall within a narrower range of 30 to 40 centimeters. The species exhibits a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism, with females consistently growing larger than males, a pattern commonly observed in mugilid fishes where fecundity selection favors larger body size in females. The relationship between total length and body mass follows a typical power-law trajectory, and the large adult size of R. corsula positions it as one of the larger members of the genus within its native drainage basins.

Puberty in Corsula is attained at a total length of approximately 22 centimeters [Lp = approximately 22 centimeters], marking the transition from the juvenile stage to the reproductively viable sub-adult phase. At this length, individuals typically weigh about 95 grams [Wwp = about 95 grams], reflecting the substantial mass gain that must accumulate before the onset of gonadal development. Histological examinations of ovarian tissue from specimens collected in the Ganges-Brahmaputra system indicate that the first wave of vitellogenesis is initiated once females surpass this size threshold, a pattern consistent with size-based rather than strictly age-based maturation schedules. Males appear to reach puberty at a slightly smaller length, though the available data suggest the 22 centimeter mark remains a reliable benchmark for the population as a whole. This length at maturity places R. corsula on an intermediate trajectory among mugilids, slower to mature than the diminutive Chelon planiceps but faster than the larger-bodied Liza macrolepis.

Eggs of the Corsula are small and pelagic, with each fertilised ovum possessing an egg diameter of approximately 0.9 millimeters, a trait that strongly influences the ultimate wet weight of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva. Upon eclosion, the lecithotrophic larva weighs approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams], an exceptionally low mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves contained within the small, transparent egg. This tiny alevin is entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk supply during the first few days post-hatching, and the period of yolk absorption is critical for survival until the mouth opens and exogenous feeding begins. The reduced egg size and correspondingly small hatchling mass are typical of mugilids that spawn in large aggregations over open waters, where high fecundity compensates for elevated larval mortality. Field observations suggest that yolk-sac resorption is completed within 48 to 72 hours at ambient river temperatures, after which the prolarva must successfully detect and capture its first prey.

Under thermal conditions characteristic of the species' spawning grounds during the monsoon season, where water temperatures average 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Corsula is realized through a combination of clutch size and spawning frequency. Females produce approximately 959 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 959 eggs per spawning event], with larger, older females contributing disproportionately to the upper end of this range. Each individual typically undergoes approximately one spawning event per day [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per day], a pattern that maximizes total annual fecundity in the brief window of favorable hydrological conditions. This reproductive strategy, inferred from fecundity relationships established for the closely related Chelon saliens, allows R. corsula to offset the high mortality experienced by its diminutive pelagic eggs and early larval stages. The cumulative annual output is substantial, reflecting an iteroparous life-history strategy with moderate parental investment per offspring.

The maximum lifespan of Rhinomugil corsula has been estimated at approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years] under the thermal conditions of its natural environment, where the mean annual water temperature is 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C]. This longevity places the species among the longer-lived mugilids, exceeding the maximum ages reported for most congeneric species, and allows females to participate in multiple spawning seasons over their lifetime, reinforcing an iteroparous reproductive strategy that balances moderate annual fecundity against sustained reproductive output across years. Females reaching the ultimate total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters] typically weigh around 777.4 grams [Wwi = around 777.4 grams], a body mass that represents the culmination of decades of growth and resource acquisition. The consistency of the thermal regime across its core habitat appears to play a key role in supporting this slow-paced life history, as cooler, stable temperatures are associated with reduced metabolic demands and extended lifespans in many teleost fishes.
